_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for New Zealand / Aotearoa covering Polynesian voyaging and Māori settlement (~1250-1300 CE, one of last major landmasses settled by humans), Māori chiefdoms and intergroup warfare, Abel Tasman first European contact 1642, Cook voyages 1769-70, Treaty of Waitangi 1840 (founding document, British sovereignty, Māori rights, ongoing reinterpretation), New Zealand Wars 1845-72, land confiscation, gold rush, Dominion status 1907, ANZAC (Gallipoli 1915, national myth), women's suffrage 1893 (first in world), welfare state, WWII, anti-nuclear policy 1984 (ANZUS split), neoliberal reforms 1984 (Rogernomics), Treaty settlement process, Christchurch earthquake 2011, Christchurch mosque massacre 2019, COVID elimination strategy.

religion.note: Rapidly secularising (No religion now largest category, 2018 census); Anglican historically dominant (now ~7%); Catholic (~10%); Presbyterian/Methodist (Scottish settlers); Pentecostal growing; Māori Christianity (Ringatū, Rātana church, syncretic, politically important, Rātana-Labour alliance since 1936); Hinduism/Islam/Buddhism (immigration); Christchurch mosque attack March 15, 2019 (51 killed, white supremacist, galvanised gun reform/social media regulation)

ethnic_groups.name: European (Pākehā)
ethnic_groups.notes: British settlers (English/Scottish/Irish/Welsh); 'Pākehā' term (Māori word for European NZers, accepted by most, debated by some); egalitarian identity ('tall poppy syndrome', DIY culture, 'she'll be right'); All Blacks (rugby, haka, national identity); distinct from Australian ('across the ditch', 6th state joke offends); film (Lord of the Rings/Hobbit landscape, Peter Jackson, 'Wellywood'); Kiwi identity (named after flightless bird, used for people/dollar/fruit)

ethnic_groups.name: Māori
ethnic_groups.notes: Polynesian indigenous people; arrived ~1250-1300 CE (one of last places settled); te reo Māori (official language, revived from near-extinction through kōhanga reo/language nests, TV stations, immersion schools); Treaty of Waitangi 1840 (founding document, English and Māori versions differ significantly, English ceded sovereignty, Māori version retained tino rangatiratanga/self-determination, reinterpretation ongoing, Waitangi Tribunal 1975); haka (war dance, All Blacks perform Ka Mate before matches, global symbol); tā moko (facial tattoo, identity marker); whakapapa (genealogy, central to identity); marae (meeting house/community centre); land confiscation (raupatu, New Zealand Wars 1845-72, millions of acres seized, Treaty settlements process returning land/money since 1990s, >$2.5B settled); Māori renaissance (1970s-present, language/culture revival, Te Papa museum, public sector bilingualism); Māori seats in Parliament (since 1867, reserved, 7 seats); 2023 coalition government controversial (Treaty Principles Bill, rolled back co-governance, hīkoi/march against)

ethnic_groups.name: Pacific Peoples (Pasifika)
ethnic_groups.notes: Samoan (~182k, largest Pacific group), Tongan (~82k), Cook Islands Māori (~80k), Niuean (~30k), Fijian, Tokelauan, Tuvaluan; largest Polynesian city in world (Auckland, ~260k Pacific peoples); Dawn Raids 1970s (immigration crackdowns, overstayers targeted, Apology 2021 by PM Ardern); South Auckland (Manukau, Pacific heartland, economic disadvantage, rugby/music culture, church central); rugby (Pacific players dominate NZ/world rugby)

ethnic_groups.name: Asian
ethnic_groups.notes: Chinese (~250k, gold rush 1860s, poll tax 1881, apology 2002; recent PRC immigration), Indian (~240k, skilled migration), Filipino (~90k, fastest growing), Korean (~30k), Japanese; Auckland ~28% Asian; integration generally positive; housing market concerns

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Middle Eastern/Latin American/African (~1.5%); multiple ethnicity reporting common (total sums >100%); growing diversity

independence.from: Dominion status from UK; Statute of Westminster adopted 1947; Constitution Act 1986 (full independence)

country_profile.notes_unique: Women's suffrage (September 19, 1893, first country in world to grant women vote, Kate Sheppard, petitioned Parliament); Treaty of Waitangi (February 6, 1840, founding document, signed between British Crown and ~500+ Māori chiefs, English/Māori versions differ critically, sovereignty vs governance debate, Waitangi Tribunal established 1975 to address breaches, Treaty settlements process ongoing, 'partnership' principle); Nuclear-free (1984, Lange government banned nuclear ships/weapons, ANZUS alliance with US suspended, US ended defence obligations, principled stand, 1987 Nuclear Free Zone law, national pride); ANZAC (Gallipoli April 25, 1915, NZ and Australian troops, 2,779 NZ killed, ANZAC Day most sacred national day, 'lest we forget'); All Blacks (rugby union, haka, most successful international sports team, 77% win rate, national religion, unified identity); Lord of the Rings (Peter Jackson, filmed entirely in NZ, tourism 'Middle-earth', Hobbiton, Weta Workshop); haka (Ka Mate by Te Rauparaha, performed by All Blacks, globally iconic); Christchurch earthquake (February 22, 2011, 185 dead, 6.3 magnitude, rebuild ongoing); Christchurch mosque attack (March 15, 2019, white supremacist killed 51, Ardern response/headscarf/gun reform praised globally); clean green image (100% Pure campaign, but dairy farming pollution reality, agricultural emissions 48%); Māori renaissance; kiwi (flightless bird, national symbol, also NZ people/dollar/fruit); Queenstown (adventure tourism, bungee jumping invented, Lord of the Rings); sheep (once 70M vs 3M people, now 26M vs 5M, wool/meat); Jacinda Ardern (PM 2017-23, gave birth in office, Christchurch response, COVID elimination, resigned for burnout, global icon of compassionate leadership); no snakes; Rugby World Cup wins (1987, 2011, 2015)

comparative_rankings._note: Country position relative to continent and global. 'rank' = 1 is best/largest.

current_leader.name: Christopher Luxon
current_leader.title: Prime Minister
current_leader.notes: National Party; former Air New Zealand CEO; coalition with ACT/NZ First; centre-right; tax cuts; cost-of-living; rolled back Three Waters co-governance; Treaty Principles Bill (controversial, Māori opposition, hīkoi 2024); infrastructure; less climate ambition

head_of_state.name: King Charles III
head_of_state.title: King of New Zealand
head_of_state.notes: Constitutional monarch; represented by Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro (since 2021, Māori, first Māori woman in role); republic debate periodic but low priority

former_leaders.name: Chris Hipkins
former_leaders.notes: Labour; succeeded Ardern (Jan 2023); 'Chippy'; COVID response minister; 'bread and butter' platform; lost October 2023 election; brief tenure

former_leaders.name: Jacinda Ardern
former_leaders.notes: Labour; youngest female head of government (37); gave birth in office (2018, 2nd world leader ever); Christchurch mosque massacre response (March 2019, headscarf, empathy, gun reform passed 6 days later, Christchurch Call against online extremism); COVID-19 elimination strategy ('go hard and go early', managed isolation, NZ among lowest death rates); re-elected 2020 landslide; resigned January 2023 ('no longer enough in the tank'); global icon of compassionate/progressive leadership; polarising domestically (housing crisis, Three Waters, cost-of-living)

former_leaders.name: Bill English
former_leaders.notes: National; succeeded Key; lost 2017 to Ardern (NZ First coalition); longest-serving finance minister; austerity; data-driven

former_leaders.name: John Key
former_leaders.notes: National; 8 years; popular; former Merrill Lynch banker; GFC response; Christchurch earthquake rebuild; flag referendum 2016 (existing flag retained, $26M cost criticised); ponytail pulling incident; resigned voluntarily

former_leaders.name: Helen Clark
former_leaders.notes: Labour; 9 years; third female PM; civil unions; Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 (Māori outcry, led to Māori Party formation); anti-Iraq War; later UNDP administrator (2009-17); diplomatic career

former_leaders.name: David Lange
former_leaders.notes: Labour; nuclear-free policy (banned nuclear ships, ANZUS split, Oxford Union debate 'I can smell the uranium on your breath', legendary oratory); Rogernomics (Finance Minister Roger Douglas's neoliberal reforms, floated dollar, deregulated, privatised, radical); transformative but contradictory
